units: the writer of the message is taking a pastry course
the mixture swells properly while it rests
the mixture collapses once it goes into the oven
the writer says she followed the given instructions to the letter
the writer tried a different leavening agent
an experienced acquaintance offers an explanation
that explanation blames the fault on too much handling
the neighbor advises cutting the last rise short
the writer asks for a meeting before changing her method
text: I am writing about the pastry course you run in the shared hall. Since I signed up, one problem has defeated me and I cannot sort it out on my own. My dough swells beautifully while it rests, then sinks the moment it goes into the oven. I have followed your instructions to the letter. I weighed every ingredient. I even switched to a different leavening agent. A neighbor of mine, who has kneaded bread since she was a girl, offered an explanation of her own. The dough gets worked too hard, she says, and the structure holding it up eventually gives way. She suggests I knead with a lighter hand and cut the second rise short. Before I try anything, I would value your judgment, since nobody knows the ovens in that hall as well as you do. If you could spare me a few minutes after the next session, I would be truly grateful.

units: the text sets two ways of cooking fish against each other
cooking over coals dries the surface and colors it
steaming keeps the moisture in the flesh
coals add a smoky aroma that the other method lacks
steam lets the clean smell of the product come through
cooking on a grill calls for a thin film of fat
cooking under a lid needs no fat at all
firm flesh suits fierce heat better
delicate flesh falls apart and has to be watched closely
text: Should a fish go over hot coals or into steam? The gap between the two is narrower than people assume, though the results never match. Coals dry the outside and color it, and they drive the juices deep into the flesh. Steam works the other way around, plumping the fibers and holding the moisture exactly where it started. What about flavor? Charcoal leaves a smoky note that steam will never produce, while steam lets the clean smell of the fish come through unmasked, with nothing laid over it. And fat? A grill wants a thin film of it, or the skin welds itself to the bars. Cooking under a lid wants none at all. So which one? Whichever suits the piece in front of you. Firm flesh takes the hard heat and comes off whole. Delicate flesh falls apart above boiling water and has to be watched closely from the first minute to the last.

units: a vegetable seller gives advice on cutting
he says the cut changes with the plant
onion has to be sliced into thin strips so that it melts
herbs are cut fine without being crushed
garlic is reduced almost to a paste so that it spreads better
carrot is prepared either in shreds or in even cubes
he warns against anything in between for that vegetable
he warns that a dull blade damages the vegetables
he advises putting an edge on the blade before a long session
text: The vegetable seller looked up from his stall last night and told me that nobody cuts everything the same way. That, he reckons, is where most people go wrong before they even light the stove. Onion has to be sliced into thin strips, thin enough to see through, or it will never melt down in the pan. Herbs you snip with the tip of the blade, never crushing them, since crushed leaves go dark and lose their smell. Garlic he likes chopped almost to a paste, because it spreads right through a sauce that way. And carrot? He laughed at that one. Shred it, or cut it into even cubes, but nothing in between. Then he handed me my change with one last piece of advice. A dull blade bruises vegetables far worse than a clumsy hand, so put an edge on it before any long session of chopping, on a wet stone, and never in a rush.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food comes before the arrival of artificial cold
drying in the air was the first technique
salt pulls the water out of flesh and halts decay
smoke above a fire makes meat keep longer
smoked meat takes on a harsh taste
traveling sellers spread these stores along long roads
kitchens far apart took up identical methods
sinking meat in melted fat seals it away from the air
these methods survive in the recipes of today
text: Long before artificial cold, keeping food edible meant a running fight against damp and rot. The earliest cooks hung their catch out in the moving air and let the wind dry it through. Later they learned that salt pulls the water out of flesh and halts decay before it starts. Then came smoke. A cut of meat left hanging above a fire took on a harsh taste and kept for whole seasons afterward. Traveling sellers carried such stores along longer and longer roads, until kitchens that had never met were working by identical methods. Later still, cooked meat sunk in melted fat sat sealed away from the air. Every step pushed back the day a food would spoil, and every one of them left a mark in the recipes we still use, repeated by cooks who never stop to wonder where the habit came from.

units: a pale foam appears on the surface of a liquid as it cooks
that foam comes from proteins released by the heat
the released particles are too light to sink back
the bubbles carry these particles upward
leaving that foam clouds the broth
a clouded broth turns gray and tastes heavier
the cook lifts it away with a ladle again and again
beating an egg white stretches the same proteins
the net that forms holds the air
a trace of salt weakens the bonds and makes the foam firmer
text: When water shivers in the pot, a pale foam climbs to the surface and clings to the sides of it. That is scum, made of the proteins the heat has driven out of the food. It rises because cooking loosens the fibers and frees particles too light to sink again, and the bubbles carry them up with them. Leave it there and it falls back into the broth and clouds it. The liquid turns gray, the taste grows heavy and dull. So a careful cook lifts it away with a ladle, patiently, as often as it forms again. Something very close to this happens under a whisk in a bowl of egg white. The beating stretches those same proteins into a supple net that traps the air. A trace of salt hurries the change along, because it weakens the bonds and lets the foam set sooner, firmer and far steadier under the spoon.

units: a fish stock had a metallic bitterness
the cook first suspected an acid ingredient and then his pot
he went back through every step of his preparation
the carcasses had boiled far too long
a short infusion without a rolling boil is what is needed
a long extraction releases sulfur compounds
the gelatin breaks down past that limit
he now rinses the carcasses and takes out the gills
he keeps the pot below boiling point
the stocks he gets are clear and free of bitterness
text: It began with a fish stock that gave off a bitter, metallic edge, the day before a service in a staff canteen. The cook blamed the vinegar first, then the pot he had used, before he walked back through his own recipe step by step. The fault lay in the bones. He had let them boil for close to an hour, when a carcass takes only a short infusion that barely trembles. Past that point the bones give up sulfur compounds and the gelatin breaks down. So he rewrote his method. He now rinses the bones in cold water, pulls out the gills, heats the pot without ever letting it reach a boil, and stops the extraction before the liquid can bubble. He strains it through fine cloth. His stocks come out clear since that correction, the bitter note is gone, and his team reports no further fault.

units: the recipe offers two tools for grinding herbs
the leaves have to be washed dried and stripped of their stems
with the mortar the salt and garlic are crushed first
the leaves go in a little at a time and are not pounded
the mortar gives a thicker and more fragrant texture
the color holds better by that route
the electric machine is used in short pulses
the bowl has to be chilled so the heat does not cook the herbs
the oil is poured in a thin stream at the end
a dry cheese may be added in fine shreds
text: Before making an herb paste, decide between the mortar and the electric machine, because the two of them do not give the same texture at all. Begin by washing the leaves, drying them thoroughly, and stripping away the tough stems. If you choose the mortar, crush the salt with the garlic first, add the leaves a handful at a time, and turn the pestle rather than pound with it. The paste will come out thicker and more fragrant, and its color will hold better. If you prefer the electric bowl, work in short pulses and chill the bowl beforehand, or the heat of the blades will cook the leaves and dull the whole thing. Either way, pour the oil in a thin stream right at the end. You may then grate a dry cheese over the top and fold it in with a fork, lightly, until the paste is even throughout.

units: a covered market has opened again after renovation work
the hall takes its light through the roof
the vegetable stalls now hold the middle of the space
the fishmongers aisle has cooling that needs no ice
part of the building is set aside for producers who transform food
a baker shapes his dough in front of the customers
a shared kitchen is offered for rent by the hour
the traders approve of the ventilation and the drainage
those two faults used to force repeated closures
future rents worry the sellers because the amount is not known
text: The covered market in the northern district opened again this week, after a refit that ran for the better part of a season. Visitors step first into a hall lit from the roof, where the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground. Beyond them runs the fishmongers aisle, cooled by a quiet system that has replaced the trays of melting ice. A third of the building has gone to producers who work on site: a baker shaping dough in front of the customers, a seasonal cannery, a cutting room. Management also announces a shared kitchen, rented by the hour, open to caterers with no premises of their own. Traders questioned there praise the ventilation and the drainage, two faults that used to force repeated closures. What worries them is the rent, whose final figure has yet to be announced.

units: steam makes it impossible to see on entering the room
the fat melts in the bottom of the pot
the pieces of meat start to brown along their edges
a caramel smell signals that liquid has to go in
the stuck juices are scraped loose and the flame is lowered
a fragrant steam escapes from under the lid
that smell travels as far as the hallway
the sauce darkens and coats the spoon
the meat gives without any effort
the heat is turned off and the smell lingers in the house
text: You walk into the kitchen and you can barely see a thing, because the steam has covered everything in sight. At first the pot says nothing. It heats, the fat melts down in the bottom, and the pieces of meat start to brown along their edges. A little later there is a burnt sugar smell in the air, and that is your signal. Pour in the liquid, scrape the stuck juices loose, drop the flame. After that everything slows. The lid shakes, one bubble breaks, another follows, and a thick fragrant steam escapes through the gap and drifts out into the hallway. Toward the end the sauce has darkened and coats the spoon, and the meat gives under the fork without any push at all. You taste, you fix the salt, you add a turn of pepper. Then you kill the heat, and the smell keeps hold of the whole house.

units: the writer refuses to treat home cooking as an optional pastime
where handing the skills down disappears industrial food takes the place
the consequences show up later at the doctors
with no adult to pass it on the child never handles a blade
the child does not learn to judge when something is cooked
grown up he buys dishes to reheat
spending on food goes up
the range of foods narrows
added sugar becomes the reference flavor
the writer judges that the cost at school would be offset by savings on care
text: We should stop treating home cooking as an optional pastime. Where the handing down of these skills fades, industrial food fills the gap, and the results turn up later in the doctors surgeries. The chain is almost mechanical. With no adult to pass on the order of operations, a child never handles a blade, never tastes a dish while it is still cooking, and never learns to judge when something is done. Grown and on his own, he buys what can be reheated, because that is the only route he controls. Spending on food climbs, variety collapses, and added sugar becomes the flavor everything else is measured against. Making such workshops compulsory at school would cost a great deal, and nobody denies it. But the savings on long term care would outrun the bill, and the generation after would win back an independence it had lost.
